title: Cornelius and Cyprian (16 September)
hookLine: a pope and a bishop, friends who disagreed and both died as martyrs

lines: TWO CITIES, A SEA, A STACK OF LETTERS.
WHAT DO YOU DO WITH THEM?
cards: A stack of letters, crossing the sea between two cities. One writer is Cornelius, bishop of Rome. The other is Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, in North Africa.
A persecution has just eased. Christians had been ordered to sacrifice to the Roman gods, and some gave in to save their lives. Now those same people are at the church door, asking to come back in.
What do you do with them? Two bishops had to answer that together, and they didn't always see it the same way.

teach.b: The people at the door were called the lapsed: those who had fallen. Some in the Church said never: once you deny Christ, the Church cannot take you back.
A Roman priest named Novatian took that line so hard that he set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome. Others said: let them all back in, no questions.
Cornelius chose a middle way: welcome them home, after a time of penance. Mercy, without pretending nothing happened.
The friendship didn't start smoothly. When Cornelius was chosen, Cyprian held back at first, waiting to be sure the choice was sound. Then he backed him firmly, and wrote to him as a brother.
On the lapsed, Cyprian had begun stricter, and with other bishops he worked his way to a path close to Cornelius's. Friends who disagreed, and kept writing.
Cyprian wrote a whole treatise on the unity of the Church, with images like rays from one sun and branches from one tree.
Paul's line in the Douay-Rheims could stand over both men: "Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Then both were taken.
Cornelius was sent into exile and died there, and the Church honors him as a martyr. Cyprian was arrested later and tried.
The account of his trial says that when the sentence of death was read, he answered: Deo gratias.

teach.h: THE UNITY OF THE SPIRIT IN THE BOND OF PEACE.
teach.b: Thanks be to God. In the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass, their names are said side by side. Still together.

how: Catholics keep Saints Cornelius and Cyprian together on 16 September, and both names are said in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass.

o: those who denied the faith under persecution
those who were baptized late in life
bishops removed from office by Rome

games.q: Cornelius and Cyprian — tap the pairs.
p: those who gave in under persecution

s: Cornelius and Cyprian agreed from the start

Cornelius welcomed the lapsed back after penance
a middle way between refusing them forever and asking nothing at all.
their names are said together in the Roman Canon
the first Eucharistic Prayer names Cornelius, then Cyprian.

games.q: you're a bishop after the persecution. people who sacrificed to the gods to save their lives are asking to come back. what do you do?
o: refuse them for good: they denied Christ.
welcome them back, after a time of penance.
let them all back at once, no questions.
games.why: Cornelius took the middle way, and Cyprian came to stand close to him. Novatian refused them, and set himself up as a rival bishop.

practice: These two kept their friendship going on paper, so choose someone whose views rub against yours and begin a silent letter: Dear, and their name.
First line, one thing in them you honestly respect; second line, one place you see it differently, said plainly, without heat; then stop, with no third line about who's right.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Lapsed, the word for those who had denied the faith under persecution and wanted back in. Cornelius and Cyprian, bishops of Rome and Carthage, disagreed on how to welcome them, and both died for the faith.

orig.note: Latin: thanks be to God. the account of Cyprian's trial gives it as his answer to the sentence of death.

carryVoice: Your line: friends who disagreed. They kept writing, and they're still named side by side. See you tomorrow.
